newsitem.title: BULGARIA: Low mark gives Bulgaria room to manoeuvre.
newsitem.headline: Low mark gives Bulgaria room to manoeuvre.

text.p: Bulgaria's currency board system anchoring the lev to the mark to stabilise the economy will benefit from the mark's weakness against the dollar, a central banker said on Thursday.
"The depreciation of the mark against the dollar gives us more room to move while observing the rules of the currency board mechanism," central bank board member Rumen Avramov told a banking seminar.

On July 1, Bulgaria introduced the IMF-prescribed system which requires all levs in circulation, bank deposits and current accounts to be fully covered by foreign exchange reserves. The lev was pegged at an exchange rate of 1,000 per mark.
The recent decline of the mark versus the dollar was favourable for Bulgarian business as most transactions in the country and abroad remained in dollars, economists say.
Bulgaria's foreign exchange reserves, which stood at three billion marks on July 4, gained from conversion of their dollar component into marks.
On Thursday the mark gained against the dollar after Bundesbank President Hans Tietmeyer said the dollar recovery was at its end and that mark strength was important in the run-up to monetary union.
Banks now had excess lev liquidity which was reflected in falling interest rates, said Avramov, urging banks to lend with caution.
"Banks have suffered from uncontrolled lending in the past years and have learned their lesson, but now they should find a way to extend credit to the economy," said Avramov.
Extravagant lending and economic mismanagement in the past seven years led to bank closures and a drastic fall of the lev earlier this year.
The currency board, which prohibits central bank lending to commercial banks and the government, restricts money operations on the local market.
A ban on central bank open market operations coupled with the fixed exchange rate regime has narrowed market instruments for regulating commercial banks' liquidity to interest rates.
The annual main interest rate was cut to 6.96 percent from 9.76 percent on Wednesday.
But commercial bankers said lending was still risky as most of the economy remained unrestructured and inefficient.

"No one can provide guarantees that a loan extended under perfect conditions with a perfect collateral will not turn into a non-performing loan in six months due to external factors," said Postbank deputy director Evgeni Petrov. -- Sofia Newsroom, 359-2-981-4145
